title: Foundations
summary: The vocabulary and mental models everything else builds on: identity vs. authentication vs. authorization, sessions, and how to read the diagrams in this repository.

lessons.title: Identity, authentication, and authorization
lessons.objective: Tell apart the three ideas people most often conflate.
lessons.content:
Three distinct questions sit at the heart of every access decision:

Identity — who are you? A claim to be a particular principal (a person, a service, a device). An identifier like a username or a sub claim names the identity; it is not proof.

Authentication (authN) — can you prove it? Verifying the claim with one or more factors: something you know (password), have (a passkey, a token), or are (biometric). The output is a trusted assertion that this principal is present.

Authorization (authZ) — what are you allowed to do? Given a proven identity, deciding whether a specific action on a specific resource is permitted. Roles, attributes, relationships, and policy live here.

The order matters: you authenticate first to establish who, then authorize to decide what. A system can authenticate you perfectly and still deny you — that is authorization doing its job.

lessons.title: How to read the diagrams
lessons.objective: Get fluent in the three views every flow uses.
lessons.content:
Most flows in this library are drawn three ways, and each answers a different question:

Sequence — the messages exchanged over time, in order. Best for “what actually goes over the wire, and in what order?”

Swimlane — the same flow with one lane per actor (User, Browser, IdP, API…). Best for “who is responsible for each step?”

Flowchart — the decision and error logic, with every deny/error path drawn explicitly. Best for “where can this fail, and what gates each outcome?”

Each flow folder also carries a Status badge — ✅ Current, 🟡 Legacy, ⛔ Deprecated, 🔵 Emerging — so you can tell at a glance whether a mechanism is something to build on or something to migrate off.

lessons.title: Sessions and tokens
lessons.objective: Understand how a system remembers you after you authenticate.
lessons.content:
Authentication happens once, but you make many requests. Something has to carry the “I already proved who I am” signal on each one. Two broad approaches:

Server-side session — the server stores session state and hands the browser an opaque session cookie. Each request sends the cookie; the server looks up the session. Easy to revoke (delete the session), but the server holds state.

Token — the client holds a signed token (often a JWT) that carries claims the server can verify without a lookup. Stateless and scalable, but harder to revoke before expiry — which is why short lifetimes, refresh rotation, and mechanisms like introspection and CAE exist.

The interactive Flow Explorer lets you step through a real token flow and see exactly what each request carries.

quiz.q: A user signs in successfully but gets a 403 when opening the admin page. Which stage denied them?
quiz.explain: They proved who they are (authentication succeeded); the system then decided this proven identity may not perform this action — that is authorization.

quiz.q: You want to know exactly which HTTP requests a flow makes and in what order. Which diagram view is best?
quiz.explain: The sequence diagram shows the ordered messages exchanged over time. Swimlane shows responsibilities; flowchart shows decision/error logic.

quiz.q: Which statement about server-side sessions vs. tokens is correct?
choices: Tokens are always more secure than sessions
Server-side sessions are easy to revoke; stateless tokens are harder to revoke before they expire
Session cookies cannot be used with HTTPS
JWTs are stored on the server, not the client
quiz.explain: Deleting a server-side session revokes it immediately. A stateless JWT stays valid until it expires, which is why short lifetimes, refresh rotation, introspection, and CAE exist.

quiz.q: A diagram carries a ⛔ Deprecated status badge. What does that signal?
choices: It is the newest, recommended approach
It is actively discouraged; prefer the linked alternative
It is still the default for new builds
It has not been reviewed yet
quiz.explain: ⛔ Deprecated means the mechanism is discouraged for new work and the page points to what to use instead (e.g. the OIDC Implicit flow → Authorization Code + PKCE).
